name: Bromus
common_group: Bromes — compare 4 installed species and native vs introduced risks
look_here_first: BROMES: separate a true BRANCHING PANICLE from a single spike and take ONE MULTIFLOWERED SPIKELET. Identify four installed species by WHOLE rooted duration and measured, backlit reproductive parts. JAPANESE annual flexuous/kinked, LANCEOLATE annual unusually long many-flowered (~25–50 mm), WOODLAND native perennial shaded broad-leaved, TEXAS native annual short-awn/1+3 GLUME-VEIN combination. Also compare introduced RESCUEGRASS (B. catharticus; not installed): wide FLAT keeled spikelets, tiny/absent awns.

priority: Whole rooted plant: annual vs perennial, and habitat only as support
Panicle architecture: straight vs kinked branches and drooping only supporting
Whole mature spikelet: 15–25 mm Japanese, 25–50 lanceolate, often ~20 Texas, ~20–40 broad flat rescue; ranges overlap
One mature lemma and its AWN, photographed/measured at 1 mm scale
Lower vs upper GLUME veins, especially Texas Brome 1 vs 3, rescue broad multi-veined
Leaf sheath hairs plus true ligule under hand lens, not inferred from distant image

comparison_lesson.title: Four installed Bromus + rescuegrass practical crew key
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: JAPANESE: kinked/drop annual. LANCEOLATE: giant many-flowered spear. WOODLAND: perennial broad soft foliage. TEXAS: native annual, 1- and 3-veined glumes. RESCUE: big flat, little or NO awn.
quick_split: Japanese brome · Bromus japonicus (introduced) — Winter annual; thin arching/kinked drooping branches; spikelets often 15–25 mm with ~6–11 florets; divergent/bent awns ~8–13 mm.
Lanceolate brome · Bromus lanceolatus (introduced) — Annual with conspicuously long pointed many-flowered spikelets ~25–50 mm, often 8–20 florets; lemma 12–18 mm, awn 6–12 mm.
Hairy woodland brome · Bromus pubescens (native broadly; county unaudited) — Perennial, wide soft foliage, frequently hairy sheaths, many-flowered heads with short straighter awns ~3–8 mm.
Texas brome · Bromus texensis (native Texas; county unaudited) — Annual with slender open sometimes few-spikeleted panicle; lemma ~9–12 mm, awn ~6–10 mm, lower glume 1 vein, upper 3.

Rescuegrass · Bromus catharticus (COMPARISON ONLY, introduced) — Open or drooping panicle with relatively large strongly flattened broad, oatlike spikelets typically ~20–40 mm; one lemma awn usually absent or very SHORT, often 0–4 mm.
guardrails: The four preexisting canonical species remain the ONLY installed Bromus species; rescuegrass is a researched comparison, not a new card.
Native or introduced state status does NOT certify Hays County; no nativity files modified.
Japanese brome typical spikelet updated to 15–25 mm based on Oklahoma State; do not use 10–15 as hard cutoff.
Actual measured glume/lemma/awn macros missing. The only preexisting arrows point to gross observed photo structures; rescuegrass new photo has NO false macro arrows.
field_sequence: Same-plant whole flowering panicle plus rooted annual/perennial crown, 1-cm ruler.
One mature complete spikelet from several branches at 1-mm scale with individual florets counted.
Separate lower/upper GLUMES backlit showing actual nerve count and measurable endpoints.
Mature lemma body and AWN in one focus plane, awn attached just below/to apex, and any two tip teeth.
True leaf blade–sheath collar, membranous ligule and sheath hairs on the same photographed culm.
For rescuegrass comparison, SHOW spikelet from face and side to confirm strong flattening and a really SHORT/absent awn.

key_characters: Annual cool-season bunch grass; senesces after seed set.
Panicle often open or nodding with thin flexuous branches, sometimes conspicuously kinked.
Spikelets often ~10–15 mm (excluding awns), usually containing several (about 6–11) florets.
Lemma awns frequently longer than on woodland brome, sometimes ~15 mm; lengths overlap other annual bromes.
Soft retrorse hairs on lower sheaths and often bent lower culms.
comparisons.against_group: Compared to B. lanceolatus, usually shorter spikelets with fewer florets and more relaxed/kinked drooping branches; lanceolatus often has ~25–50 mm spikelets with 8–20 florets. Compared to native B. texensis, note Texas brome generally shorter 6–10 mm awns and requires lemma/branch dissection, not habitat alone. Unlike perennial B. pubescens, this is an annual and usually shorter-lived.

key_characters: Annual grass with often ascending or spreading branches, less filmy and flexuous than Japanese brome.
Lanceolate to oblong elongated spikelets often ~25–50 mm with 8–20 florets, much larger than typical Japanese brome.
Mature fertile lemma usually ~12–18 mm and awned around 6–12 mm in GrassBase treatment; measurements overlap.
Membranous ligule, hairy to nearly smooth sheaths, variable leaf-blade pubescence.
Awn arises from notched lemma tip; detailed shape/length and glume nerves require hand lens.
comparisons.against_group: B. japonicus has often smaller ~10–15 mm spikelets and a delicate, sometimes kinked drooping panicle. Native B. texensis often has 9–12 mm lemmas and 6–10 mm awns, but forms overlap; determine on mature dissected spikelets. B. pubescens is perennial and has broad softer foliage, relatively short straight awns and an open drooping woodland panicle.

key_characters: Perennial in shady moist woods rather than short-lived cool-season weed.
Erect to arching leafy culms often 0.6–1.5 m high, with relatively broad 6–19 mm grass blades.
Open spreading/drooping panicle generally ~10–25 cm long.
Multi-flowered spikelets ~13–30 mm, often with 5–10 florets.
Lemma short straight awn usually ~3–8 mm; surfaces often fine-hairy, but this cannot be confirmed from current photo.
Closed sheaths with soft retrorse hairs, ligule short membranous; botanical treatments differ slightly in typical lengths.
comparisons.against_group: Unlike the three other currently installed Bromus cards, B. pubescens is PERENNIAL and often found in shaded moist woodland understory. Japanese brome is a small-spikeleted annual with flexuous panicle branches; B. lanceolatus has unusually long, many-flowered annual spikelets; B. texensis is an annual with shorter awns and requires mature glume/lemma comparison. Habitat or hairiness alone cannot clinch this one.

key_characters: Annual (not perennial) native Texas brome of open woodland/grassland sites.
Sheaths with soft recurved/retrorse hairs; blades often ~3–7 mm wide.
Fertile lemmas typically ~9–12 mm, with a two-toothed apex and one 6–10 mm awn.
Spikelets multi-flowered, borne on branching panicle.
Fertilizing yellow anthers may be conspicuous at flowering, but are common to other grass taxa.
comparisons.against_group: B. japonicus is an introduced annual with often smaller 10–15 mm spikelets, longer awns and more flexuous nodding branches. B. lanceolatus has often much larger many-flowered spikelets and longer lemmas. B. pubescens is a perennial of moist shady woods with broader leaves. All split characters require scale: green, slender spikelets alone are not enough for native vs introduced labels.

comparison_matrix.title: Bromus: five-way species diagnosis, not native from silhouette
rows: Winter annual; thin arching/kinked drooping branches; spikelets often 15–25 mm with ~6–11 florets; divergent/bent awns ~8–13 mm.
Entire panicle BRANCHES + 2–3 mature awned spikelets, lower sheath, measure lemma and awn. Kinked long-pediceled loose head + divergent awns favors Japanese; never declare invasive from size alone.
Annual with conspicuously long pointed many-flowered spikelets ~25–50 mm, often 8–20 florets; lemma 12–18 mm, awn 6–12 mm.
Mature WHOLE long spikelets and florets counted against a millimeter ruler. Long spear of overlapping florets with clear awns, not broad flattened oat-shaped head, raises lanceolate.
Hairy woodland brome · Bromus pubescens (native broadly; county unaudited)
Perennial, wide soft foliage, frequently hairy sheaths, many-flowered heads with short straighter awns ~3–8 mm.

Rooted OLD CROWN + broad softer leaf, drooping shaded-woodland panicle and mature spikelet. A true persistent perennial woodland bunch supports pubescens; mature spikelet and awn detail still required.
Texas brome · Bromus texensis (native Texas; county unaudited)
Annual with slender open sometimes few-spikeleted panicle; lemma ~9–12 mm, awn ~6–10 mm, lower glume 1 vein, upper 3.
Mature lemma and true first/second glumes on one intact spikelet with 1-mm scale and backlight. Glume vein count and measured awn/lemma are the decisive follow-up before native/invasive decision.
Open or drooping panicle with relatively large strongly flattened broad, oatlike spikelets typically ~20–40 mm; one lemma awn usually absent or very SHORT, often 0–4 mm.
Turn one mature spikelet SIDEWAYS, inspect its flat keel and lemma awn length. Large flat boat-shaped spikelet + absent or tiny awns → rescuegrass candidate; preserve photo specimen until verified.

what_to_teach_crew: Count FLORETS stacked along a single Bromus spikelet; distinguish from barley's one-flowered triad and wildrye's multi-flowered spikelets on a single long spike.
Do not rely on head droop: most bromes can droop with maturity, moisture or height.
A large seedhead may be native Texas brome, introduced lanceolate or rescuegrass; turn the spikelet SIDEWAYS to check compression and awn length.
For introduced Japanese versus native Texas brome, compare mm-measured lemmas/awns and 1 vs 3 glume veins, not 15 versus 20 mm alone.
Texas brome has rare, specific county voucher records in historical taxonomic literature; local county range status must be audited separately before restoration claims.
Record the actual source photograph licenses; long ago one-photo gallery coverage is NOT botanical completion.

items.label: Existing Japanese brome photo
items.image_role: Original physically stored and pixel-inspected species-labelled photograph; IDs remain based on the credited source determination
items.caption: Archived source photograph shows green awned spikelets held against fingers, with arching fine panicle branches. It does NOT show the true ligule or basal sheaths.
items.why_it_matters: Cool-season INTRODUCED annual; slender drooping and kinked panicle branches with groups of several relatively small (about 10–15 mm) multi-flowered awned spikelets. Lower sheaths often soft-haired. Do not identify it by awns alone.
items.creator: Alexey P. Seregin

items.caption: Original archive shows multiple long green many-flowered spikelets against rocky background; exact mm measurements are NOT derivable from the image.
items.why_it_matters: Introduced Mediterranean-region annual; check the LONG, narrow lance-shaped many-flowered spikelets (often roughly 25–50 mm) on an open branching panicle. For separation from other bromes, count florets and check the mature awn insertion and lemma-tip teeth with magnification.

items.label: Existing Texas brome photo
items.image_role: Original physically stored and pixel-inspected species-labelled photograph; IDs remain based on the credited source determination
items.caption: Original species-tagged flowering photograph clearly shows narrow green spikelets, long fine projecting awns, and protruding yellow anthers. Does NOT show basal hair or exact lemma teeth.
items.why_it_matters: Native Texas annual; inspect mature green elongated narrow spikelets with several florets. Lemma bodies are commonly 9–12 mm, with an awn around 6–10 mm and slightly 2-toothed tip; measure glume, lemma, and awn to rule out introduced Japanese and lanceolate bromes. Flowering yellow anthers can be visible, but are NOT species-specific.

items.label: Rescuegrass — broad flattened, almost awnless spikelets (COMPARISON ONLY)
items.image_role: John Tann Commons species-identified real Australian rescuegrass plant photo; gross flowering habit and branched drooping panicle, macro features not resolved
items.caption: Rescuegrass is an introduced winter grass with relatively large broad, strongly flattened wedge- or oat-shaped spikelets. The individual fertile lemmas have very short awns, or none, unlike the clearly long-awed Japanese brome and other local bromes. The photo is an Australian source; no spikelet-level arrow is placed without pixel validation.
items.why_it_matters: A rescuegrass candidate with a large, distinctly flat spikelet and little/no obvious awn should not be called Japanese or native Texas brome merely by its nodding panicle.
items.creator: John Tann
items.photo_status: Flickr-review-confirmed Commons CC BY 2.0 and taxon-source metadata. Photo is not a magnified dissected spikelet, so no new structural marker claims; comparison only, never counted as installed species.
